title: Inflight Mutation Guards and Toolchain Compatibility Shim for Multi-step Tool Execution
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Problem:
Multi-tool chains in the Core API are increasingly used by customers for streaming workflows and function/tool calling. We observe two related failure modes in production and in e2e tests: 1) tool result injection that mutates shared request context causes unbounded recursive re-invocation (user prompt -> tool A -> inject -> tool B -> injection triggers tool A again), and 2) older tool adapters (compatibility layer) do not honor the new structured-output contract, leading to malformed injections that bypass loop protections.

Impact:
- Latency spikes and token storming for affected sessions.
- Higher GPU utilization and billing surprises for customers with chained workflows.
- Risk of data leakage via improperly sanitized injected results.

Goals / Acceptance criteria:
1) Prevent unbounded recursion triggered by injected tool output while preserving legitimate multi-step flows.
2) Provide a short-term compatibility shim that normalizes results from legacy tool adapters to the structured-output contract used by the runtime.
3) Maintain streaming semantics and minimal latency for common fast-path chains (single-hop tool -> output -> client).
4) Expose metrics and tracing for loops detected, depth per session, and number of normalizations performed.

Proposed design (high level):
- Inflight Mutation Guard: attach a lightweight provenance envelope to any tool-produced injection (fields: origin_tool, sequence_id, hop_count). Hop_count incremented on every injection observation. The runtime enforces a max_hops threshold (configurable per-customer) and returns a explicit structured error (type: loop_detected) to the caller when exceeded.
- Idempotency Passport: each tool-run result carries an idempotency token derived from (origin_tool, canonicalized_payload_hash). The runtime rejects replays of identical injection payloads that would cause re-triggering within the same request session window (default 30s).
- Compatibility shim: for legacy adapters that emit free-text or pre-structured blobs, introduce an adapter-level sanitizer that attempts to coerce results to the current structured-output schema (fields: kind, payload, provenance). Shim runs in the adapter layer and returns a normalized envelope or a soft-failure with a hint to caller (structured_error: compatibility_normalization_failed).
- Streaming considerations: when streaming tool results into an ongoing response, the guard checks hop_count on chunk boundaries. If a chunk signals a loop, the stream emits a final control event and closes gracefully instead of leaving the client hanging.
- Observability: add traces for each injection event (trace tags: injection.hop, injection.origin, injection.normalized). Add counters: injection.loop_detected_total, injection.normalized_total, injection.replay_rejected_total. Surface these in Console under per-route telemetry.

Implementation plan (phases):
Phase 1 (1 sprint) - Prototype guard and shim in the dev routing cluster:
- Implement envelope and hop_count checks in the call graph layer (runtime gateway).
- Add idempotency passport verification for same-session replays.
- Build a minimal compatibility shim for the two oldest adapters (legacy-webhook, legacy-dbtool).
- Add unit tests and integration tests (e2e chain sims).
Phase 2 (2 sprints) - Harden and rollout:
- Expand shim coverage to other adapters, add feature flag for per-customer toggles.
- Add streaming chunk-level handling and graceful control events for clients.
- Add metrics and Console widgets for per-route injection telemetry.
Phase 3 - Documentation + client SDK updates:
- Publish API contract update and migration guide for adapter authors.
- Ship SDK helpers for generating idempotency passport and canonical payload hashing.

Trade-offs and alternatives considered:
- Option to drop injections entirely for N hops and return partial results (rejected as breaking UX for many customers).
- Strong schema enforcement at ingestion time (rejected because some partners still depend on legacy free-text payloads; shim gives a migration path).
- Centralized global hop limit versus per-customer configurable limit (choose per-customer for flexibility; default global safe value = 4).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Define canonicalization algorithm for payload hashing (should ignore transient timestamps and ephemeral session ids). Owner: @Mateo.
- Finalize default max_hops value and expose UI controls in Console. Product to confirm.
- Performance benchmark: measure additional p50/p95 tail introduced by shim for fast-path chains. Infra to run load test.
